analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal tax credit for private donations that fund private school scholarships.
analysis.headline: The repeal bill was introduced in June 2026 with 105 Democratic cosponsors, referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, and has not received a markup or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Current law gives donors a federal tax credit for giving to scholarship organizations that pay private school tuition, and lets families exclude those scholarships from their taxable income. This bill repeals both provisions after 2026. Its backers argue the credit drains federal money that would otherwise support public schools; its opponents say it helps families pay for private schooling.
analysis.who_benefits: Public schools and their students, because the federal subsidy pipeline for private school scholarships would close. Taxpayers generally also gain, since tax credits for donations would no longer reduce federal revenue.

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes section 25F of the tax code, ending the credit individuals can claim for contributing to scholarship granting organizations, effective for tax years ending after December 31, 2026.
It also strikes section 139K, which currently excludes private school scholarship amounts received by families from gross income, for amounts received after December 31, 2026.

With those repeals, money that was being channeled out of the federal treasury toward private school tuition stays available to fund public obligations, which the bill's title frames as keeping public funds in public schools.

analysis.who_pays: Donors who use the tax credit to offset their federal taxes, the scholarship granting organizations that receive the contributions, and families who rely on those scholarships or the income-tax exclusion for them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private school donors, scholarship organizations, and recipient families

drawbacks.text: Families receiving private school scholarships would lose the tax-free treatment of that scholarship money for amounts received after the end of 2026, raising their taxable income.
Donors would no longer be able to claim the credit for contributions to scholarship granting organizations for tax years ending after 2026, removing a financial incentive the current law created.

A good-faith objection from school-choice supporters is that these scholarships let some families leave public schools they believe are not serving their children; repeal closes that route rather than fixing the underlying schools. The bill text does not address how affected students' educational needs would be met.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The repeal protects federal revenue and public school funding, but it does so by taking away a subsidy that some families use to pay private school tuition, and those families bear the loss directly. The bill offers no transition or replacement support for them. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how much one values the public-school funding argument versus the school-choice benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Ways and Means Committee in June 2026, and nothing has happened since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Gwen Moore of Wisconsin introduced the bill on June 11, 2026, with 74 other original cosponsors listed in the bill text.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which has jurisdiction over tax credits.
The cosponsor list later grew to 105 House Democrats, all from one party; no Republicans are listed as cosponsors.
Since the June 11 referral, the action history shows no further steps — no committee markup has been scheduled and the bill has not reached the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the scholarship-granting organization industry and donors using the credit keep their subsidy, because the committee majority has taken no action on the repeal.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Donors and scholarship groups keep the subsidy for now

for.name: Rep. Gwen Moore
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the scholarship tax credit and the scholarship income exclusion.

for.name: 105 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the repeal bill.

against.name: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee chair with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 11, 2026; the record shows no markup, hearing, or floor action since.

sides.party_line_note: All 105 cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republican cosponsor appears on the list, and the Republican-controlled Ways and Means Committee has taken no action since the referral.

industries.industry: Scholarship granting organizations (private school scholarship funds)
industries.note: These organizations exist to collect donor money and pay private school tuition; the federal tax credit is the engine that attracts their donations, and repeal shuts that pipeline down after 2026.
The credit expands the pool of tuition-paying families, so repeal reduces a demand subsidy for private schools; schools themselves are not directly regulated, but the customer pipeline narrows.

industries.industry: High-income donors who use the credit
industries.note: A tax credit of this kind rewards donors with a dollar-for-dollar reduction in federal tax owed; repeal removes that benefit, and the revenue stays with the treasury instead of subsidizing private tuition.
Repeal keeps the subsidy from being claimed against federal revenue, which backers argue preserves funding capacity for public schools serving all students.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits with a Ways and Means Committee whose majority created the credit it would repeal; with no Republican cosponsors and no markup scheduled months after referral, the realistic path is that it stays in committee and expires at the end of this Congress in January 2027.
